newsitem.title: UK: Doubts over Busang hurt gold exploration sector.
newsitem.headline: Doubts over Busang hurt gold exploration sector.

text.p: The discovery of the fabulous Busang gold deposit was a siren call to explorers and investors, and news that it may not be as rich as previously stated is a painful blow to the sector, analysts said on Thursday.
"This is likely to undermine confidence in the gold sector in general, and junior exploration stocks in particular," said analyst Nick Hatch of Flemings Global Mining Group.
At an estimated 71 million ounces, the Indonesian deposit had been touted as the biggest gold discovery this century.
But the mining world was stunned on Wednesday when Bre-X Minerals Ltd., the Canadian exploration company which discovered Busang, admitted that test samples may have been overstated.
Bre-X's partner, Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold, said separately that drilling results so far "indicate insignificant amounts of gold."
The statements helped boost the price of gold modestly, but the gains were shortlived and dealers said the market had shrugged off the news by Thursday morning.
More significantly, shares in Bre-X were halted on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Wednesday and nervous investors dumped stocks in other junior mining companies.
Some share prices have tumbled by 20 and 40 percent on the news, analysts said, and more losses were expected.

"It's going to be a fairly volatile time until we see exactly what happened," said Martin Rosser a director at David Williamson Associates, a London-based consulting firm specialising in mining and minerals industries.

"This will make it harder to attract new money into the business in terms of financing from instutional investors, because they understandably will be reluctant to get exposure to the sector until they get a picture of what went wrong."
Venturesome junior mining companies, most of them Canadian, have lately been at the forefront of gold exploration in newly accessible, less developed countries.
Busang's promise of fabulous riches was held up as the model of exploration success, and indirectly helped attract millions of investment dollars into exploration.
Analysts estimate that spending on mining exploration was some $4-$5 billion last year, with emerging markets, such as Indonesia, seeing the biggest explosion in growth.
The extent of the backlash from the Busang news is still unclear, although it is obvious potential investors will demand more rigour in the assaying and sampling process of deposits, Rosser said.
"These markets tend to be resilient," Rosser said.

"The problem is that now people are going to have to take time have their confidence rebuilt. If it turns out Busang has 50 million ounces rather than 70 million, that's bad but not a major disaster, But if it's 10 million, then something really awful has happened," he added.
But the blow to investor confidence from Busang may have a positive effect on the sector in the long run, Hatch said.
"Valuations on junior explorers operating outside of North America are likely to come back to more reasonable levels, allowing for more reasonably priced acquisitions by majors," he said.
